I really like the mystery of Fanatic, and I hope the mystery remains.

The beautiful thing of her character (and religion in general) is the balance of choosing to believe in something unprovable, with the acceptance that you could be wrong.

That struggle of Faith, when approached honestly, reveals ourselves and the world in really interesting ways, and when approached fearfully or self-centeredly leads us the wrong way, many times a very wrong way.

Long way of saying I hope in the end the answer to her power source is not fully known.

I'm splitting hairs perhaps but for me there is an important distinction between "Her power is her faith granted by the Divine" and "Her power is her faith, unlocked by some outside force that is defined but not Divine"

 

In both cases, her faith and her belief are her power. This is an indisputable fact of the character because when her faith wavers, she is weakened and when it is firm her strength increases. No matter what the truth of the source of the power that allows her to utilize her faith, she is powered by that belief and faith.

 

And, personally, it changes nothing about her actions either way. She has (potentially) done some really horrible things, things that she has had to confront many times. She has killed, she was destroyed, all in the name of a greater good, but these are still sins she must confront. Looking at the region she grew up in, she's 99% likely to be Roman Catholic or some minor variation on that. She probably goes to confessionals a lot, she spends lots of times in meditation, confirming whether or not she believes she did what she needed to do while sticking to her faith as best she could. 

 

And, again personally, I would consider her discovering her powers do not come directly from God to be the ultimate test of her faith. Fanatic is the only Good Angel we are aware of, if she finds out the power she was granted came from this Host of evil or at least dangerous beings, could that not also have been God's will? God, according to the Churches, is Infinite, Omniscient, and works in mysterious ways. Having this Host accidentally give her the power, creating a warrior of virtue and honor who could stand against them, seems like a very "god-like" thing for him to do. But, it is a test for her, finding out she does not have God's Mandate to act as she has would shake her more than anything else she could have discovered or found out, and would lead almost directly to the PW Fanatic story arc. She doesn't know her place in the world, but that doesn't mean she can allow evil to run free. There is a chance that she is wrong about the nature of her power, but that does not mean she is wrong in using that power in God's name.

 

 

But, I can see how this is all splitting hairs. It's a tight-rope and I'm honestly eager to see what Christopher and Adam reveal about all this and the way they have handled such tricky balancing.

posts.name: phantaskippy
posts.cooked:
Fanatic having Faith based powers that were granted by something known is incredibly problematic.  You cannot have Faith in things you know are true, that is definitionally impossible.  And if she has powers from element F that are based on her own faith, then the internal reality of her character becomes power through self-delusion.  

Fanatic knows she has powers through real things, but has to believe in other things in order to use that power, so there is no pursuit of knowledge, no soul searching, her ability to fight is her ability to not question, to supress her own mind.

That may work, but man, that internal struggle is not engaging.  "Oh no, I thought too much, and now I am going to lose, if only there was a handy brainwashing kit nearby"

Or if her power is known to be faith in herself, then her struggle becomes against irrational doubt, which could be engaging if the character struggled with depression or anxiety, but even then her growth and failure would have a known solution internal to herself, and that is more of a short arc than a long term quest.

I know these are off the cuff examples, but my point is that fact and faith can't interact like that.  When you know something, you can't believe in it, you can't hope for it.  Fanatic is a walking crisis of faith, what is right, what is wrong, what am I, why am I this person, all these unknowns that she carries with her are her.  I would love to see C&A surprise me by pulling off an engaging story that keeps alive an engaging struggle of Faith while resolving the Faith itself, but I haven't seen it accomplished yet.

I guess the weird thing is that in Catholicism, while faith is important, grace is more achieved through the state of being a good Catholic in doing God's work via charity, helping people, affirming and saving life, using your skills to better the world, etc., and because these deeds mean you're using your grace to further God's work and grow closer to His perfection, He grants you more grace to use. I know this is kind of de-railing things, but man do I find this an interesting discussion.

 

I think the question of Faith vs Knowing is more confusing.

 

I think I'm going to reference Michael Carpenter of the Dresden Files. In fact, the Dresden Files in general does this whole thing very well. We meet Archangels who speak of God, but we never meet God himself. Also, the magic of those people who are people of Faith is immense and subtle in ways that Harry acknowledges but can hardly believe.

 

There is a scene in one of the books where Micheal and HArry have to go on some dangerous mission. Harry tries to convince Micheal not to go, or at least delay, because someone has to watch over Micheal's family. Micheal sighs and opens the front door, where a mutual friend is standing, just about to knock, because his car broke down right in front of their house and he was hoping he could come in and stay for a bit.

 

At a certain point, having divinely granted power, having a divinely mandated sword, speaking with Angels, and having things work out in inesplicable ways, it would take a madman to say that someone or something isn't looking out for that person. It would take a far stretch to say that Micheal acts solely on Faith with no evidence, he has plenty of evidence that he has been chosen for a mission and that some limited protection has been granted him and his family because of it. When he retires due to injuries, there is a small squad of angels that simply patrol around his house, protecting them from supernatural threats.

 

They know God is on their side, and many people even in our world would say they know. That there is plenty of evidence to support their Faith without them having to meet an angel or meet God himself.

 

Fanatic doesn't need faith in herself, she has faith that God will support her and carry her through the toughest of trials. She doesn't need to delude herself, even if she discovers that her powers would accidentally given to her by a hostile alien force, that does not mean that the accident which created her was not God's will. She has clearly done good work in the name of the Lord, so her Faith does not need to become a false faith.

 

It's not a very difficult step to take that many of the heroes came about because of a similiar situation to her own. What force led Blake Washington Jr or Anthony Drake to these very specific artifacts which unlocked thier potential and made them into hereos who protected thousands of people? How was it that Mainstay and Medico just happened to be exposed to a material that granted them power, before any of their villains or monsters also got that same power? The Parson line has been blessed has it not? How did Ryan Frost survive an accident which clearly should have claimed his life?

 

Eventually the answer to these questions (in a world not in a story) narrows down to two possibilities. Random Chance in a universe of spiraling numbers or Divine Will of something greater.

 

Getting to the point of accepting that it is Divine Will is the challenge, it is the part of this which Fanatic must take on faith, and that is not a bad thing to be reduced to that point.

 

 

As for the conflict between her and Idolater, I'm really interested in learning what it is that he did. He pulled off some grand betrayal of the people or of Fanatic herself, something which drove her to mark him. The church burning was a result of their battle, obviously, but I'd love to know their relationship.

 

And her expression, to me, says more "I did what had to be done, may I find forgiveness for those actions" and less "I did this terrible thing because of my mission"

 

She knows what she did was terrible, and I really hope that Fanatic was rarely a character who fell onto the terror of "God demands I do this so it is right, even if it is a terrible crime" because that is the dark side of Faith, that is where all the evils of religion breed and spread from. I'd like to think her faith is more geniune. She has done terrible things in the pursuit of the greater good, but she never lies to herself and says that they were not evil or terrible. Instead, she seeks to make sure that the good of her actions outweighs the evil, that she seeks forgiveness whenever possible and makes recompense even more often.

 

 

Again, I'm really excited to learn more about her. I feel like Fanatic is one of the least understood heroes in the entire game, and this makes her fascinating to consider the possibilities.

The problem is that this would open up a big can of worms that 100% absolutely exists in real life as well: Why is God only on the side of certain good people, then, while other equally good people are left to suffer and struggle?

To quote a bit of my favorite Babylon 5 dialogue:

"I used to think it was awful that life was so unfair. Then I thought, 'wouldn't it be much worse if life were fair, and all the terrible things that happen to us come because we actually deserve them?' So now I take great comfort in the general hostility and unfairness of the universe."

Honestly this was a factor in my own deliberations on faith; I had seen too much suffering inflicted on good people while the people who hurt them prospered, too many good people with terrible luck and bad people with grand luck, to want to believe in a world where that sort of thing was planned and enforced by a divine entity as opposed to just being how the world as created by us mortals worked and therefore something us mortals could possibly actually fix to make right.

Hence, you know, one reason why I tried to politely say I didn't feel like this was a thing I wanted opened up.

The problem is that this would open up a big can of worms that 100% absolutely exists in real life as well: Why is God only on the side of certain good people, then, while other equally good people are left to suffer and struggle?To quote a bit of my favorite Babylon 5 dialogue:"I used to think it was awful that life was so unfair. Then I thought, 'wouldn't it be much worse if life *were* fair, and all the terrible things that happen to us come because we actually deserve them?' So now I take great comfort in the general hostility and unfairness of the universe."Honestly this was a factor in my own deliberations on faith; I had seen too much suffering inflicted on good people while the people who hurt them prospered, too many good people with terrible luck and bad people with grand luck, to want to believe in a world where that sort of thing was planned and enforced by a divine entity as opposed to just being how the world as created by us mortals worked and therefore something us mortals could possibly actually fix to make right.Hence, you know, one reason why I tried to politely say I didn't feel like this was a thing I wanted opened up.

 

Oh I completely agree about the real world, but I find faith and spirituality a fascinating literary device to explore.

 

In terms of the Dresden Verse, the reason "God" helps the Carpenter family in more obvious ways is because Micheal is the wielder of one of the Three Holy Swords of that world. Thus Micheal has been given a burden to fight vampires, dragons, 13 fallen angels, ect ect ect, and so making sure he has a babysitter is kind of small potatoes compared to the burden he has been given.

 

But, once more, I'm talking literature and fantasy worlds, I like considering these questions with that buffer and with the freedom to change the various conditions to explore the questions from various angles.

There is a scene in one of the books where Micheal and HArry have to go on some dangerous mission. Harry tries to convince Micheal not to go, or at least delay, because someone has to watch over Micheal's family. Micheal sighs and opens the front door, where a mutual friend is standing, just about to knock, because his car broke down right in front of their house and he was hoping he could come in and stay for a bit. At a certain point, having divinely granted power, having a divinely mandated sword, speaking with Angels, and having things work out in inesplicable ways, it would take a madman to say that someone or something isn't looking out for that person. It would take a far stretch to say that Micheal acts solely on Faith with no evidence, he has plenty of evidence that he has been chosen for a mission and that some limited protection has been granted him and his family because of it. When he retires due to injuries, there is a small squad of angels that simply patrol around his house, protecting them from supernatural threats. They know God is on their side, and many people even in our world would say they know. That there is plenty of evidence to support their Faith without them having to meet an angel or meet God himself.

 

I LOVE the Dresden Files. Part of what i find interresting is that Michael's whole power source is boiled down to, to quote Harry, "He's a Rigtious man." Because when your faith is rewarded again and again it really is that simple. Michael knows that he has an ability to protect other people so it's his duty to do so, because other people can't. He wouldn't shirk from that even if his faith in God were questionable. And because he would act in uh… good faith?.. anyway he recieves these blessings and help.

 

On the other hand if we look at one of the other Knights of the Cross from those books, Sanya if i remember his name right; is an Agnostic. Yep, he's weilding a holy saber with a nail from the Crucifiction, captial C in his hand guard, and he's a self described Agnostic. But Sanya still gets the same divine grace and assistance as Michael because he is working towards the same goals in good faith but for different reasons. He's a Comunist. That's why he keeps stepping into danger for other people works to fight the things that go bump in the night; Because as a Comunist everyone has a job for the good of the people & this is his.
